html:
The Zambezi is the fourth-longest river in Africa, about 2,570 kilometres long, and the largest African river flowing into the Indian Ocean. It rises in northwestern Zambia and runs through Angola, along the borders of Zambia, Namibia, Botswana and Zimbabwe, and across Mozambique to the sea.

In its upper course it floods a wide plain each year, the home of the Lozi kingdom, whose king moves to higher ground in a great canoe procession. Downstream it plunges over Victoria Falls, called Mosi-oa-Tunya, "the smoke that thunders", then runs through deep gorges.

The river was a road and a barrier. From the 1500s Portuguese traders went upriver to Sena and Tete to deal with the gold-rich kingdom of Mutapa. In the 1830s the Ngoni crossed the Zambezi heading north, fleeing the wars in the south. David Livingstone reached the falls in 1855 and hoped the river would be a highway for trade and Christianity, but his expedition of 1858 to 1864 found the Cahora Bassa rapids blocked the way.

In the colonial era it became a source of power and a crossing for railways:

  • The Victoria Falls Bridge of 1905 carried the railway north from Rhodesia.
  • The Kariba Dam of 1959 made one of the world's largest reservoirs and forced tens of thousands of Tonga people from their homes.
  • The Cahora Bassa dam in Mozambique followed in the 1970s.
